# Indriyavibhaṅga (Vb 5)

**ID:** Vb 5
**Section:** Vibhaṅga (vb)
**Collection:** Abhidhamma
**Title (Pali):** Indriyavibhaṅga
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/vb5
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/abh02m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Indriyavibhaṅga* ("Analysis of Faculties") is the fifth treatise of the *Vibhaṅga*, the second book of the Theravāda Abhidhamma Piṭaka [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. Unlike most chapters of the *Vibhaṅga*, it does not contain a Suttanta analysis (*suttantabhājanīya*), but consists solely of an Abhidhamma analysis (*abhidhammabhājanīya*) followed by a catechetical interrogation section (*pañhāvāra*) [Bodhi 2003; Gethin 2001; Nyanatiloka 2007]. Scholars observe that while the specific faculties were extracted from the discourses, the complete assemblage of the twenty-two faculties into a standalone classification rubric belongs to the early Abhidhamma methodology rather than a unified discourse-level category [Bodhi 2003].

The treatise expounds twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) covering sensory, physical, affective, spiritual, and supramundane domains [Nyanatiloka 2007; Hazra 1994]. These comprise the six sense faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind), femininity (*itthindriya*), masculinity (*purisindriya*), the life faculty (*jīvitindriya*), five faculties of feeling (*sukha*, *dukkha*, *somanassa*, *domanassa*, *upekkhā*), the five spiritual faculties (*saddhā*, *viriya*, *sati*, *samādhi*, *paññā*), and three supramundane faculties pertaining to gnosis [Hazra 1994; Nyanatiloka 2007]. The Abhidhamma analysis consists of definitional registers for each of the twenty-two faculties; the registers for the five spiritual faculties match the equivalent analyses found in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, aligning faculties with corresponding spiritual powers (*bala*) and path factors [Gethin 2001]. Traditional Theravāda commentators, such as Ledi Sayadaw, highlight its role alongside discourse collections like the *Indriya Saṁyutta* in systematically detailing the cultivation of spiritual faculties [Ledi Sayadaw 1971].

Cross-textual connections noted by SuttaCentral include the *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33), the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* (Vb 18), the *Puggalapaññatti* (Pp 1.1), and the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects extensive Pali-internal text reuse with earlier *Vibhaṅga* books—especially the *Khandhavibhaṅga* (Vb 1), *Āyatanavibhaṅga* (Vb 2), *Dhātuvibhaṅga* (Vb 3), and *Saccavibhaṅga* (Vb 4)—as well as the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, *Paṭṭhāna*, and *Indriya Saṁyutta* (SN 48) [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language alignments, DharmaNexus identifies shared material with northern Buddhist treatises on the faculties, notably Vasubandhu's *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and *Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa*, Ghoṣaka's *Abhidharmāmṛta*, the Sanskrit and Tibetan versions of the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* (along with its *Nibandhana*), and the Chinese *Ekottarika Āgama* [DharmaNexus].
